transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2026-02-25
Start: 15:30 UTC
Duration: ~52 minutes
Attendees: Lena Ortiz (Redwood AE), Marcus Huang (Redwood SE), Diego Ramos (Redwood), Priya Desai (Antares ML), Tom Reynolds (Antares Infra), Sophia Kim (Antares CTO), Evan Moore (Antares SRE)

Summary:
Quick technical deep dive focusing on quantization tradeoffs (INT8/FP8/GPTQ/AWQ), observed accuracy regressions on Antares workloads, and runtime/perf implications for Dedicated or Private deployments (VPC). Agreed next steps to run bench matrix and share configs.

[00:00] Lena: Hey everybody, thanks for joining, uh I think we have about 50 minutes, we wanted to do a deep dive on the quantization options and how they impact latency/throughput and quality for the Antares usecases. Marcus is gonna lead the bench/technical bits.
[00:18] Marcus: Hey all, quick agenda; first recap of Antares constraints, then go over INT8 vs FP8 vs GPTQ vs AWQ, talk about runtime things - batching, KV cache, kernel selection, then open Q&A. Sound good?
[00:28] Priya: Yep that works for us, main goal is to get to a configuration that keeps production p95 latency under 400ms for 7B with comparable quality to our FP16 baseline. We also have strong throughput needs for batch scoring during off-peak.
[00:42] Tom: And we need it in our VPC; cannot send data to hosted, need private control plane or dedicated capacity. SOC2 requirements as well.
[00:50] Lena: Noted. We'll cover Dedicated and Private options and what that means for KMS and audit logs. Marcus?
[01:02] Marcus: Cool. So high level: INT8 (e.g., 8-bit quant via bitsandbytes or fused kernels) is the low hanging fruit — good perf win typically 2-3x speedup and large mem reduction but depends on layernorm sensitivity. GPTQ and AWQ are post-training quant methods that can hit lower bitwidths, often 4-bit-ish effective, with varying accuracy. FP8 is emerging for training/inference on newest stacks but support is spotty across runtimes and GPUs.
[01:35] Sophia: Quick question — we've seen AWQ advertised as almost lossless on some 7B models, is that consistent?
[01:41] Marcus: Good question. AWQ often preserves quality well for a subset of weights by using asymmetric quantization and per-channel scales, but it isn't magic — it depends on model topology and activation distributions. For some causal LM heads you can see sub-1% perplexity delta; for other tasks like code generation or summarization it can be more pronounced. We recommend a prompt-level eval.
[02:06] Priya: We care about rouge/ROUGE-like metrics and also hallucination rates. If AWQ changes token probabilities slightly it can amplify hallucinations in our pipelines.
[02:15] Marcus: Totally. That's why our suggest is bench on your real prompts and measure both generation quality and calibration (nll) across temperature sweeps.
[02:28] Evan: On the runtime side, how does KV cache interact with quantized weights? Does the cache get quantized too?
[02:36] Marcus: The KV cache is separate — it's activations/memory and we keep that in FP16 or FP32 in the runtime. The quantization affects the model weights and kernel paths. There are some experimental approaches to compressing KV cache but that adds decode/encode overhead and can hurt latency. For p95 SLOs we typically keep KV in FP16.
[02:56] Tom: So the big latency wins come from smaller weights (less memory moves) and faster matmul kernels?
[03:02] Marcus: Exactly. Kernel selection matters. Our runtime has a compiler/kernel selector that chooses the fastest kernel given model shape, sequence len, and bitwidth. For INT8 we use fused GEMM kernels; for GPTQ/AWQ we sometimes fall back to custom kernels that have more ops per token.
[03:22] Priya: In your benchmarks, what's the tradeoff p95 vs throughput? If we tune batching aggressively will we blow our latency SLOs?
[03:30] Marcus: There's a predictable curve. For small interactive requests, we keep batch size 1 with micro-batching and async scheduling to keep p95 low. For throughput windows (night batch scoring) we push larger batch sizes and rely on KV prefix caching to reduce work. We can also do smart routing — route latency-critical requests to FP16/dedicated hot pool and batch scoring to a cheaper quantized pool.
[03:52] Sophia: What about FP8? We have some Hopper A100X stuff coming — would FP8 be better than AWQ?
[03:58] Marcus: FP8 can be great where hardware supports it natively (newer NV hardware and certain compiler stacks). FP8 is still floating and can be more forgiving than INT4/8 fixed-point, but you need full stack support (compilers, kernels, and model export). In practice for now FP8 is a bit experimental; AWQ/GPTQ have broader community tooling like bitsandbytes/GPTQ libraries.
[04:23] Tom: Do you have numbers for p50/p95 for 7B on Dedicated with INT8 vs GPTQ vs AWQ?
[04:29] Marcus: I have rough numbers from our internal bench — 7B causal model, seq len 64, batch 1: FP16 p50 ~60ms p95 ~140ms on an L40; INT8 fused kernels p50 ~30ms p95 ~80ms; GPTQ/AWQ implementations (depending on kernel maturity) p50 ~35-45ms p95 ~90-130ms. These are synthetic — your shape and prompt will change them.
[04:55] Priya: That's helpful. We'll need those runs on our real prompts. Also curious about memory— will 7B fit on a single 40GB GPU when quantized?
[05:06] Marcus: Usually yes for INT8/GPTQ; AWQ may be slightly bigger depending on per-channel scaling metadata. For 7B, INT8 often reduces peak memory to under 20GB with KV in FP16. GPTQ sometimes uses extra offline reordering storage but still fits. We'll confirm with runs.
[05:25] Evan: Any gotchas for Private/VPC deployment? Does quantization affect encryption/KMS flows?
[05:30] Lena: No effect on KMS; quantized weights are just files. For Private you manage network and keys, and Redwood's Private control plane supports HSM/KMS integrations. We do need to ensure image/container runtime has the quant kernels and drivers — our onboarding checklist covers that.
[05:46] Tom: About accuracy regressions — have you seen systematic patterns where INT8 breaks certain attention heads or layernorm?
[05:52] Marcus: Yes, layernorm and embedding tables are sensitive. Common approach: keep layernorm/embedding/softmax in FP16 while quantizing large matmuls. GPTQ/AWQ often leave certain layers higher precision or apply per-channel scaling to mitigate. The resulting hybrid model is usually the best compromise.
[06:12] Priya: Can Redwood runtime do hybrid precision automatically or do we need to produce a hybrid artifact?
[06:18] Marcus: We support both. We can ingest GPTQ/AWQ artifacts and the runtime will use the provided dtype maps. We also have automated traces that suggest layers to keep in FP16; we can run an autotune to produce a hybrid artifact. That said if you're using a community toolchain you might provide the model and we can host it as-is.
[06:36] Sophia: How do you validate generation quality at scale? We have thousands of prompts and fine-grained metrics.
[06:42] Marcus: We recommend a dataset-driven eval — run your prompt set across FP16 and quantized variants, compute nll/delta, token-level KL and generation metrics (BLEU/ROUGE/EM depending). For hallucination we add adversarial prompts. Redwood Optimize can help with regression alerts and per-prompt diffs.
[06:59] Priya: Would love to see diffs per prompt; that helps trust.
[07:02] Lena: We'll include per-prompt delta tables in the bench results.
[07:08] Evan: Operationally, what about fallbacks — if a quantized kernel errors at runtime can you auto-fallback to FP16?
[07:14] Marcus: Yes, runtime has graceful fallback policies. We can route requests to a fallback pool or transparently run FP16 path for specific model endpoints. That costs more but keeps availability. We also do canary rollouts for any new quant artifact.
[07:29] Tom: On the subject of throughputs and batching: what are suggested autoscaling/batch policy knobs for our Dedicated pool?
[07:36] Marcus: Use a combination: target utilization threshold (e.g., 65%) to spin up more instances, max batch latency (e.g., 20ms) for interactive endpoints, and separate pools for interactive vs batch scoring. Also leverage prefix KV caching for repeated prompts to reduce tokens computed.
[07:53] Priya: What's prefix/KV caching behavior with dynamic prompts? We have many prompt prefixes.
[07:58] Marcus: Caching works best when prompts share prefixes—like system messages or common instruction templates. For highly dynamic prompts caching helps less. We can do per-route caching TTLs and fingerprinting to trade memory vs hit rate.
[08:12] Sophia: Any recommendations on model selection? We were looking at LlamaX-ish and some custom fine-tuned weights.
[08:18] Marcus: If you have a fine-tuned weight, quantize the final artifact and run the same pipeline — sometimes fine-tuning accentuates sensitivity. For base models, we have vetted variants in the Redwood catalog with performance profiles; often the best path is pick a model with similar architecture to those validated by GPTQ/AWQ community.
[08:36] Priya: For the bench matrix — can you include both end-to-end latency (from client SDK) and pure inference times?
[08:41] Marcus: Absolutely; we'll capture client-to-response p50/p95, and token generation throughput.
[08:46] Tom: Any notes on GPU selection? We're leaning towards L40s but have access to H100s in some clouds.
[08:52] Marcus: H100s are great for FP8 and some fused kernels; L40 and A100 are great for INT8/GPTQ/AWQ in production today. H100 can give better latency for FP16/FP8 but cost is higher. We'll include cost/perf estimates.
[09:07] Priya: For the AWQ/GPTQ toolchain, any recommended repos or versions to use to produce artifacts compatible with Redwood?
[09:13] Marcus: We recommend the community GPTQ forks that output Redwood-compatible artifacts, and AWQ releases after 0.8 are fairly stable. We also support bitsandbytes quant and the usual transformers pipeline. We'll send a compatibility matrix with exact commit hashes.
[09:29] Sophia: How long does conversion take per model?
[09:33] Marcus: Depends on model size and hardware — for 7B on an 80GB GPU conversion/GPTQ usually takes a couple hours; AWQ can be similar. We parallelize where possible.
[09:43] Evan: Is there an impact on warm-start/first-token latency after deploy?
[09:48] Marcus: First token often includes model setup and cache warmup; quantized models may have slightly longer cold starts if extra transpose/permute steps are required. We mitigate with pre-warm strategies and keeping a hot pool.
[10:02] Priya: Any real-world examples where quantization introduced subtle regression only visible in long-form generation?
[10:08] Marcus: Yes; we've seen cases where quantization slightly biases repetition penalties or softmax tails leading to degenerate long generations. That's why per-length evals and temperature sweeps are important.
[10:20] Lena: Okay I want to make sure we capture the ask: Antares wants p95 < 400ms for 7B interactive, similar generation quality to FP16, fits in VPC for compliance. We'll run bench matrix across FP16, INT8, GPTQ, AWQ on Antares prompts. Marcus and Diego to produce configs. Anything else?
[10:36] Priya: One more operational: do you expose per-token cost breakdowns in Redwood Console when using quantized models?
[10:41] Lena: Yes, we show token-level cost and latency breakdowns; quantized pools will show lower per-token cost estimates.
[10:48] Tom: We'll need audit logs and SSO enabled before pilot.
[10:51] Lena: Noted, we'll send the security checklist.
[10:55] Marcus: I'll add one more technical note — for GPTQ there's sometimes a need to reorder weights and use specific kernels; that can require a one-time conversion step that our runtime caches. Also watch out for tokenizer differences during quant generations.
[11:12] Priya: Great, thanks. Can you push the bench results and the diffs per prompt?
[11:17] Lena: Yes. We'll aim for initial bench deliverable in about a week.
[11:22] Sophia: Thanks everyone, that was helpful.
[11:25] Lena: Thanks all — we'll follow up with the artifact links and schedule the pilot call after the bench.

Meeting end.
